objective.text: Use place value to relate neighbouring base ten units from millions to thousandths.

explanations.title: One tenth as large
explanations.text: Dividing a unit by ten gives the next smaller unit. One million divided by ten is one hundred thousand. One tenth divided by ten is one hundredth.

explanations.title: A new unit: thousandths
explanations.text: The pattern goes on past hundredths. One hundredth divided by ten is one thousandth. Ten thousandths make one hundredth.

explanations.title: Times ten moves digits left
explanations.text: Multiply 4 tenths by ten to get 40 tenths. That is 4 ones. Ten tenths are bundled into one, so the digit moves one place left.

explanations.title: Divide by ten moves digits right
explanations.text: Divide 6 by ten and the 6 becomes 6 tenths. Each digit is one tenth as large, so it moves one place right.

hints.text: Draw the place value chart. Put each digit in its own place.
Multiplying by ten moves every digit one place to the left. Dividing moves it right.
Count the zeros in the number you multiply or divide by. That tells how many places the digits move.
The exponent tells how many tens are multiplied together. It matches the zeros.
Say the unit name. Then use a basic fact with that unit.
Think how many small units fit in a big unit. Then multiply or divide.
Add or subtract like units. Tenths with tenths, hundredths with hundredths.
Trade ten of a small unit for one of the next larger unit.
Compare digits from the left. Find the first place where they differ.
Rename both numbers with the same unit. Then compare.
Find the nearest numbers on each side for that place. Then check if you are past the halfway point.
Round the numbers and estimate first. Then place the decimal point.
Draw an area model. Multiply each unit by the whole number. Then add the partial products.
If you cannot share a unit evenly, trade it for ten of the next smaller unit.
Draw a tape diagram. Label the total and the parts.
Divide like whole numbers first. Then think about the unit to place the decimal point.
